pairs.oneshot_text:
Based on the evidence provided, here is a synthesis of how American cities changed from 1980 to 2024 regarding gentrification, inequality, affordability, and displacement.

### Gentrification
Gentrification has accelerated significantly since 1980, with the most rapid changes occurring after the year 2000. Research indicates that gentrification levels were at their lowest in the 1970s but increased every decade until 2010 [Source: ev-10]. The rate of gentrification doubled between the 1990s and the period following the 200 Census; while only 9% of neighborhoods experienced gentrification in the 1990, nearly 20% did so from 200 onward [Source: ev-1].

By definition used in recent studies, gentrifying tracts are those with initially low median household income and home values (bottom 40th percentile) that subsequently saw increases in inflation-adjusted home values and educational attainment (bachelor’s degrees) placing them in the top third of their metro area [Source: ev-1]. Academically, this is categorized into three types:
*   **Income Gentrification:** Neighborhoods where household incomes rose faster than the metropolitan average. This was rare in the 197s–80s but became dominant by the 200s [Source: ev-10; Source: ev-11].
*   **Educational Gentrification:** An increase in college-educated residents outpacing the metro rate [Source: ev-10].
*   **Occupational Gentrification:** An increase in professional occupations outpacing the metro rate. This was most common in the 197os but grew less rapidly over time compared to income and educational gentrification [Source: ev-10].

Geographically, gentrification is concentrated in specific regions. Portland, OR saw the highest share of eligible tracts gentrify (58.1%), followed by Washington D.C. (51.9%), Minneapolis (50.6%), and Seattle (50%) [Source: ev-1; Source: ev-11]. In contrast, cities like Detroit, El Paso, and Las Vegas experienced practically no gentrification [Source: ev-1]. Nationally, however, gentrification remains rare, affecting only 8% of all neighborhoods reviewed since the 2000 Census [Source: ev-1].

Demographically, gentrifying neighborhoods recorded population increases and became wher, with the non-Hispanic white share increasing an average of 4.3 percentage points [Source: ev-1]. Conversely, lower-income areas that did not gentrify saw slight population losses and a concentration of minorities [Source: ev-1]. This shift is part of a broader trend where urban cores have become more diverse; while whites remain the majority nationally, they are now a minority in most urban counties (53% are majority nonwhite) compared to suburban or rural areas [Source: ev-7; Source: ev-11]. The migration of young adults has fueled this change, as nearly 80% of the country’s growth in its under-45 population since 198 has been concentrated in metro areas with over one million residents [Source: ev-8; Source: ev-11].

### Inequality
Income inequality in American cities has widened substantially between 198 and 2024. National income inequality reached record levels by 2018–2021, with Gini coefficients rising from approximately 0.40 in 23 to 0.494 in 2021 [Source: ev-3; Source: ev-11]. Metropolitan areas generally exhibit higher inequality than the nation as a whole; for instance, in 214, the aggregate 95/20 ratio (the income of the top 5% versus the bottom 2%) was 9.7 for large metros compared to 9.3 nationally [Source: ev-5].

Major cities are hubs of extreme disparity. New York City has a Gini coefficient of 0.5469, while Atlanta and Miami reach 0.57, and New Orleans reaches 0.56 [Source: ev-2; Source: ev-11]. In terms of raw ratios, New Orleans leads major U.S. cities with an inequality ratio of 7.87, meaning the top earners make nearly eight times as much as the lowest earners [Source: ev-4; Source: ev-11]. Boston follows closely at 7.81 [Source: ev-4]. The Bridgeport metro area (New York suburb) also led lists for high inequality due to very high incomes among its top earners [Source: ev-5].

This inequality is driven by economic shifts away from manufacturing toward service industries. Manufacturing jobs fell from a peak of 19.5 million in 1979 to under 11.5 million during the pandemic, while finance and professional services soared from 12 million to 32 million [Source: ev-8; Source: ev-11]. These white-collar industries cluster in large cities like Washington D.C. and San Francisco, concentrating high-income professionals in urban cores alongside low-income service workers [Source: ev-8; Source: ev-11]. Between 2007 and 2014, inequality rose because top incomes remained stable or declined modestly while bottom incomes dropped substantially; double-digit slides in 2nd percentile incomes were common across large metros [Source: ev-5].

### Affordability
The gap between income growth and housing costs has widened for decades, creating a severe affordability crisis in major cities. From 200 to 204, median household income grew by only 92% (from $41,990 to $86,610), whereas median home prices nearly tripled, jumping 177% from $122,775 to $339,937 [Source: ev-6; Source: ev-11]. On an inflation-adjusted basis, incomes increased just 8.5%, while home prices rose more than 56% [Source: ev-6].

California dominates the list of unaffordable markets. Five of the six large U.S. cities with the highest price-to-income ratios are in California: Los Angeles (9.6–12.2 ratio range), San Jose, Long Beach, San Francisco, and San Diego [Source: ev-6; Source: ev-11]. These ratios are more than double the national average of approximately 4.6–4.7 [Source: ev-6; Source: ev-11]. Beyond California, New York City, Miami, and Boston also face extreme pressures where home prices far outpace local incomes [Source: ev-6]. The Case-Shiller Index reached 325.78 in July 2024, representing a 225% increase since January 200 [Source: ev-11].

### Displacement
Displacement is a primary consequence of gentrification, but its impact is not evenly distributed across racial lines. Research focusing on Philadelphia indicates that the negative effects are felt disproportionately by minority communities [Source: ev-9]. Specifically, financially disadvantaged residents moving from historically Black gentrifying neighborhoods tend to move to poorer, non-gentrifying neighborhoods within the city [Source: ev-9; Source: ev-11]. In contrast, poor residents moving from non-Black gentrifying areas often succeed in moving to more advantaged locations or suburbs [Source: ev-9].

This disparity exists because racially stratified housing markets and discriminatory lending practices limit options for Black residents [Source: ev-9]. As gentrification proceeds, affordable neighborhoods shrink, forcing displaced minorities into a "shrinking set of affordable yet disadvantaged neighborhoods," thereby exacerbating neighborhood inequality by race and class [Source: ev-9]. While gentrifying tracts saw poverty rates drop slightly (0.7 percentage points), non-gentrifying low-income tracts saw their poverty rates climb nearly 7 percent [Source: ev-1; Source: ev-11]. This suggests that while some areas become wealthier, the displacement pushes lower-income populations into areas with high crime and low-quality schools unless policy interventions like property tax relief or renter stability measures are implemented [Source: ev-9].
